title: What a Market Solves
description: A market solves one problem: a buyer and a seller who cannot find each other. The identical instant round trip costs 0.002 per cent of the position on one instrument and 4.5 per cent on another.

title: The Order Book
description: The order book is every resting limit order at every price, and the quote is only its top line: on an ordinary book it describes 900 shares out of 7,300. Walk a market order through it and watch slippage appear from arithmetic alone.

title: What a Fill Actually Is
description: Your order meets one specific counterparty who chose that moment to trade against you. Why that makes your fills a biased sample, and why the same one-in-ten miss rate costs one trader $1.50 and another $15.

title: The Spread Is the Price of Immediacy
description: The spread in cents tells you nothing. Divided by your stop it gives the win rate you need just to break even, from one formula: (1 + spread/stop) / 2.

title: Why Anyone Quotes At All
description: A market maker faces two risks: the position they did not want, and the customer who knows more. Watch a penny-wide quote on 2,000 shares become four cents on 300 before any news arrives.

title: The Candle Is a Summary
description: A candle keeps five numbers and discards everything else. Two intervals that produce the same five numbers can make 0.35 on one bracket and lose 0.15 on the same one.

title: Time and Sales
description: The tape carries three reported facts. The fourth, which side was the aggressor, is inferred, right about four times in five, and one wrong print of 900 shares swings a minute from +600 to −1,200.

title: Volume and Delta
description: Volume counts contracts, and every one of them was bought and sold. Delta counts who was unwilling to wait: a bar reported at +15 per cent establishes a buy share only between 50.0 and 62.5 per cent.

title: Who Else Is Here
description: Four kinds of participant, sorted by what they want rather than how big they are. On one day, $22,500 from the uninformed arrives as $5,000 for the quoters and $17,500 for the informed.

title: Every Trade Starts Negative
description: Spread, commission, slippage and financing are charged whether the trade works or not. On one $10,000 trade they total $9.29 against $120 at risk, and only $2.00 of that is the spread.

title: Slippage and Impact at Retail Size
description: What a fill costs is your size divided by the size resting in front of you. The same $30,000 costs $0.30 in one instrument and $80.00 in another, at the same instant.

title: What Should You Actually Trade
description: Rank instruments by what a round trip costs as a share of what they move in a day. An index ETF gives up 0.2% of its range; a $1.50 micro-cap gives up 52%.

title: What You Are Actually Buying
description: A share, a futures contract, an option and a perpetual are four different legal objects. On one view, the smallest position they permit runs from $500 to $250,000.

title: Margin and Leverage
description: Margin is collateral, not a measure of what a position can lose. On one worked contract the deposit is fifty times the money at risk, and at 10x leverage a 10% move is the whole of it.

title: When Your Broker Acts Without You
description: Five published rules let someone else act in your account without asking. On a position half borrowed against a 30 per cent requirement, a fall of 28.6 per cent hands the decision to your broker.

title: Sim Against Live
description: A simulator sets every cost this module measured to zero. A strategy that reports +$1,000 over a hundred trades can net minus $700 once they are put back, and the breakeven win rate moves from 50% to 58.5%.

title: Expectancy
description: An edge is a number, not a feeling about a chart. A setup winning seven times in ten can lose 0.125R a trade while one winning four times in ten makes 1.40R, from one line of arithmetic.

title: What an Edge Feels Like
description: At a 45% win rate, eight losses in a row turns up in more than half of all 200-trade samples and arrives on average every 263 trades. Streak length depends on your win rate alone. The drawdown that threatens the account is a different and larger number.

title: How Long Until You Know
description: Fifty trades cannot tell a method making 0.35R a trade apart from one with no edge at all. An edge that has halved needs 571 trades to establish, close to three years, and putting your costs back takes the first row from 143 trades to 540.

title: Position Sizing
description: Position size = (account times the fraction you risk) divided by the distance to your stop. The fraction is chosen from the drawdown you can keep trading through, not the return you want: the same one-in-twenty bad run costs 15% at 1% a trade and 39.5% at 3%, which needs a 65% gain to undo.

title: Where the Stop Goes
description: On one trade the stop with the best reward to risk at 3.00 and the lowest breakeven win rate at 25% is the one that is certainly wrong. The right stop needs 37.5%, and 44% once costs are in. The level says where the reason dies; ATR says how much room ordinary movement needs.

title: Risk of Ruin
description: Ruin is computable from three numbers you already have: your edge, the fraction you risk and how far you are allowed to fall. It is not driven by bad luck. On one winning system, risking 1% of the account halved not a single career in two hundred thousand; risking 10% halved sixteen in a hundred.

title: Keeping the Record
description: Ten fields, written down at the time, decide whether any question in this module can be answered about your own trading. On eight real trades the broker statement puts the payoff ratio at 2.16 and the record puts it at 2.51. Two of the ten cannot be recovered afterwards at any price, and a statement contains neither.

title: When the Drawdown Arrives
description: This module priced the drawdown you are in. It has not priced what you are about to do about it, and that is the larger number: at 5% a trade, sizing up returns you to the high in nine careers out of ten and digs the hole to twice its depth in nearly half of them.

title: Where Liquidity Rests
description: Stop orders are market orders that have not happened yet, and they collect at a handful of prices because the rules for placing them are few and shared. A stop 0.1 ATR below a level has the best reward to risk on the page at 9.2 to 1 and still loses money; the band that keeps 95% of the best expectancy runs from 0.47 to 0.84 ATR.

title: The Order Book Is Theater
description: A resting order costs nothing to place and nothing to withdraw, so a wall shows intent rather than commitment. The same 80/80 read is worth 2.6 points of win rate where 5 in 100 walls hold and 10.9 where 40 in 100 do, and the size of the wall enters the arithmetic nowhere.

title: The Liquidity Lie
description: Deliberate manipulation of a market is real, is prosecuted, and looks almost nothing like the version you were told. The same technique is worth $62,500 a go at a billion dollars of exposure and $25 at two contracts, and moving your stop out far enough to escape it gives up 0.46R on every trade.

title: Absorption and Exhaustion
description: When price reaches a level, volume was spent there and the level held or it did not, which is the first hard fact in this module. But two bars can share every quantity a candle records, and the volume traded at every individual price, and still carry deltas of +2,820 and -1,680 that two schools read as opposite trades.

title: Volume at Price
description: Volume at price is a count, with none of the classification a footprint needs. But the point of control is the mode of a histogram: on one 9,160-contract session four ordinary row heights put it across 9.5 ticks of a 15-tick range, and the coarsest reading turns on 21 contracts. The mean moves a sixth of a tick.

title: Volume Profile
description: A point of control slides 9.5 ticks across a 15-tick day. The value area your platform ships moves 3.5, and the one it does not ship moves one. It is still not what it says on the tin: the box labelled 70% holds anywhere from 70% to 84% depending on a setting, and widening the window from one session to two puts half of the heavier day’s value area outside value entirely.

title: Hidden Size
description: Showing size costs money, so the people with size do not show it, and the screen understates as routinely as it overstates. In a hundred tests at one level the detector could not have fired on eighty; it fired on 14 of the other 20, which bounds the rate between 14% and 94%. A quiet book multiplies your odds by 0.8.

title: Market Structure
description: A break of structure and a change of character predict something you can count, which puts them ahead of every named chart pattern. But they are computed from a swing definition that is a dial: on twenty bars the same prices hold 8 structure events, or 2, or none, and two ordinary settings disagree about who is in control on 4 bars in 12.

title: Order Blocks and Displacement
description: An order block is the last opposite-coloured candle before a strong move away from it. That sentence contains three settings and no observations. On the twenty bars of lesson 32, now with bodies, ordinary choices give ten order blocks, or five, or four, or two.

title: Divergence
description: A divergence is price disagreeing with a number computed from price. On sixty closes, ordinary settings give 3 divergences, or 2, or 1, or none, and the swing rule alone decides whether there are 33 places to look or 5. Two windows whose every bar is identical in size read 86.2 and 71.4, because the advance took seven slots instead of ten.

title: Sweeps, Beyond the First
description: A sweep is price trading past a level and coming back. Three settings decide whether one happened at all, and on the same sixty bars they find 4 sweeps or 46. Neither of the two levels that reached a second sweep stopped there: one was swept four times and one eight, and the deepest of the eight went 0.6 past a level on bars averaging 1.35.

title: Markets Have Modes
description: The crudest regime measurement is one ratio with one setting, and on sixty closes it separates the sideways stretch from the rally with no overlap. Change the window from ten closes to thirty and the two readings disagree on 22 of 30 bars. A filter keeping 3 trades in 10 turns an 8-month question into a 27-month one.

title: Detecting a Regime Change
description: Locating a change in a finished series and deciding one has happened now are different problems, and only the second is the one you have. On sixty closes, one bar of confirmation halves the changes declared from 8 to 4 and five bars halves it again, while the share of the move you stay inside goes 7, 4, 3, 2 and then 10 out of 10.

title: What a Timeframe Is
description: A bar is a rule for grouping the tape, and the rule has two settings: how wide each group is and where the first one starts. Only the first is ever quoted. Regroup sixty bars four at a time and the sample high and low do not move, while the swing count falls from 15 to 2. Move only the starting bar and the regime ratio runs from 0.104 to 0.249 on identical tape.

title: Trading More Than One
description: Three widths of the same tape agree on 9 bars in 40, which is less often than three unrelated coins with the same bias would. Requiring all three cuts 18 candidate longs to 7. A filter raises your expectancy the moment it removes any higher share of losers than winners, and raises your money only past your profit factor of 1.64.

title: Multi-Day Structure
description: Take the same sixty closes and remove the overlap and 19 of 39 transitions become gaps. The high, the low and the efficiency ratio do not move at all. The swing count is 15 both times and two of the fifteen points are at different bars. A stop inside a gap fills at a median of 1.5 times the loss it promised and 4.5 times at worst.

title: The Session Cycle
description: A session is the interval between two closures, and its edges concentrate activity for three structural reasons that have nothing to do with mood. But split this module’s sixty bars into three consecutive twenties and the efficiency ratio reads 0.021, 0.067 and 0.333 on a series with no clock in it at all.

title: Opening and Closing Auctions
description: A call auction solves for the one price at which the most shares can trade. On a book of fifteen orders it clears at 100.50, two ticks above everything that traded in the session, and charges that price on all 2,600 shares where walking the identical sell limits would have averaged 100.2654. One more seller 1,200 strong two ticks lower is worth 520 to the buyer.

title: Scheduled Events
description: An event with a date on it has a price, and the option chain quotes it. A stock at 100 with a 6.00 straddle is quoting a six per cent move — but the long call breaks even at 3.10 per cent, not six, and a stop placed inside the quote is a stop the market has already told you will be passed.

title: Volatility as a Quantity
description: The same sixty bars give a per-bar standard deviation of 0.32 per cent and of 3.43 per cent, and the difference is the window rather than the market. Where the divide-by-sixteen rule comes from, why a reading of 30 describes a 1.51 per cent day and not a 1.89 per cent one, and why a 6.00 straddle is quoting 7.52.

title: Correlation
description: Correlation is one division away from two return series, and the answer moves with the window the same way volatility did. Three exact results survive the noise: a regression slope is the correlation times a ratio of standard deviations, a hedge removes the square of the correlation, and twenty positions correlated at 0.3 carry the risk of three.

title: Positioning Data
description: The Commitments of Traders report is a census, not a leak, and the standard reading of it counts one fact twice. Net positions sum to exactly zero, so commercials at a short extreme and speculators at a long extreme are one sentence. The index everyone quotes is a range statistic that one new record week can move by 44 points.

title: The Macro Cycle
description: A release moves price by the part nobody knew, and most of a headline number was already public. Eleven of the twelve months inside an annual inflation rate were printed before it, and on the series below the rate falls 3.37 points across half a year with four fifths of that fall carried by the months leaving the window rather than the ones arriving.

title: What an Indicator Is
description: An indicator is a function of prices you already have, so it cannot add information, and what it discards can be counted. Two ten-bar windows of the same series have averages 0.09 apart and standard deviations 0.076 apart while one drifts nowhere and the other trends, at efficiency ratios of 0.053 and 0.536.

title: Repainting
description: An indicator that needs bars after the one it draws on revises what it has drawn, and the revision runs in your favour by construction. On the module’s sixty closes the same pivot rule returns 20.40 points where the finished chart shows it and 3.90 points where it was actually knowable.

title: Moving Averages as Support
description: The claim is that price finds support at a moving average. On this module’s sixty closes the ten-bar average is approached 17 times within eight tenths of a point and the price continues away on 9 of them, against 45 per cent for any bar at all — and telling those two apart would take 609 approaches. The golden cross arrives with 54 per cent of the advance behind it.

title: Oscillators Under Regime
description: Two standard implementations of the same fourteen-bar oscillator, run over this module’s sixty closes: one prints 13 readings above 70 and the other prints none. What 70 asks for is an average gain seven thirds of the average loss, which at equal move sizes is seven up bars in ten, and what follows the thirteen is 58 per cent against a base rate of 58.

title: Confirmation Bias, Measured
description: Three indicators at four lookbacks is twelve configurations, and on 20 of the 39 bars where all twelve are defined one reads bullish while another reads bearish. They correlate at 0.5455, which is 1.71 opinions, and none of the twelve beats the tape’s own 60.5 per cent.

title: What the Spread Is Paying For
description: A break-even spread is twice the chance the next order knows something, times what it knows. That line prices a penny spread at one informed order in a thousand, refuses to price a fifty-cent one at all, and says your own crossing costs $453,600 a year at sixty round trips in dime-wide markets.

title: The Fee That Routes Your Order
description: One decision sits between your button and your fill, and a published fee schedule makes it. The swing across routing outcomes is $1.65 on a 300-share order, and the access fee you never pay turns lesson 53’s $3.00 round trip into $4.80.

title: What a Millisecond Is Worth
description: A resting quote is an option, and speed is how fast you can take it back. On a large fund at 16 per cent volatility the delay at which a typical move reaches the half-cent half-spread is 21.3 milliseconds. On a small company quoted fifty cents wide it is 171 minutes.

title: The Side the Tape Leaves Out
description: An off-exchange print carries a price, a size and a venue flag, and never a side. The rule that reconstructs the side from the session average reconstructs the session instead: it tracks the day’s return at a correlation of 0.93.

title: What a Million Shares Takes
description: An institution starts a schedule, not an order. At 10 per cent of daily volume the time to finish is ten times the order’s size in days of volume, and the price risk of that wait runs from 12 to 446 times the whole spread cost of the same shares.

title: What an Order Type Gives Away
description: A market order leaves the price open and a limit order leaves the fill open, and nothing leaves neither. On this course’s sixty closes a buy limit 0.8 under the close fills 16 times in 56 and still averages a loss, because the fills are selected.

title: What Hurry Costs
description: Impact is the price of speed, not of size. Inverting the square-root law puts the threshold at 358 million dollars in an index fund and 1,050 in a micro cap, and the optimal schedule turns out to have no volatility in it at all.

title: The Flow With No Opinion
description: A dealer’s hedge is a function of price, so its trading follows. On this course’s sixty closes 10,000 contracts take 3,079,024 shares of trading to hold a position that never exceeds a million.

title: The Number You Cannot Look Up
description: The run-and-reclaim frequency moves from 0.00 to 1.00 across two definitional choices on the same sixty closes, so solve for the break-even instead: half the probability that the level simply holds.

title: What Would Have to Happen
description: After two down closes the next close is up 6 times out of 9 on this course’s sixty closes, but 54.24 per cent of all its moves close up anyway and the interval around 6 of 9 swallows both numbers, so the count settles nothing.

title: Backtesting as Evidence
description: The best of 253 moving-average rules on this course’s sixty closes beats holding by 4.16 a share after costs, and 52.5 per cent of series with no time structure at all beat it by more.

title: The Price of Looking
description: The best of 253 rules on this course’s sixty closes posts a t-statistic of 3.65. Whether that is a one-in-147 result or a coin flip turns on one number no backtest prints.

title: The Horizon You Fix First
description: A 156-trade forward test judged once passes a system with no edge 5.05 per cent of the time. Judged after every trade, the same dead system passes 24.25 per cent of the time.

title: The Benchmark You Chose
description: Lesson 63’s winning rule owes 57.7 per cent of its return to the market against a fully invested benchmark and 30.0 per cent against its own exposure. Both are right.

title: The Drawdown You Should Expect
description: A real edge of a tenth of an R a trade spends a 156-trade run inside a median worst drawdown of 8.82R. Stopping at eight R switches off 59.5 per cent of systems that work.

title: How Much the Trade Holds
description: On a twenty basis point edge the whole trade holds 29,900 dollars in the small cap and 1,050 in the micro cap. Not your share of it. Everyone in it, together.

title: The Delay You Remove
description: Five minutes between signal and order costs eight trades out of 589 on a position held a session. It is also the only thing stopping the fiftieth order.

title: Machine Learning as a Filter
description: Six hyperparameters at five values each manufactures 0.318 of an R a trade. And a filter can only give back your losers, so on a rule with six winners and one loser a perfect one would add 4.30 per cent.

title: How Many Bets You Are Carrying
description: The median correlation between two of lesson 63’s 253 rules is 0.9472 and the least alike pair is 0.4845. However many rules you add, the bets top out at 1.06.

title: The Day Every Stop Hits
description: Four positions at two per cent are eight per cent of heat, and at the measured correlation that eight per cent arrives one day in 2.5. Independent, it would be one day in 16.

title: The Weights You Can Hold
description: The optimiser wants 0.987, minus 0.438, minus 0.705 and 1.156, and 3.29 dollars of position per dollar of account. Forbidding the shorts keeps 59 per cent of the cut and all of your leverage.

title: The Window Decides
description: In one fortnight of the course’s own data, 9.50 per cent of the 31,878 rule pairs are correlated at exactly one. In the next fortnight, 72.23 per cent are.

title: Which Limit Binds First
description: The correlation columns narrow four rules to two and the heat cap says one. Four rules instead of one, at the same three per cent of heat, buys a day 2.86 per cent smaller.

title: The Pace You Actually Trade At
description: Lesson 65 assumed forty trades a month and said the forty was not derived. Measured on the grid this course has been running, 80.63 per cent of rules fire twice or less, and the book asks for nothing on fifteen days in twenty-eight.

title: The Link You Do Not Own
description: Availability along a chain multiplies, so the broker is a ceiling you cannot buy past. A stop resting at the broker moves an open position from 96.3 unprotected hours a year to 8.8, and costs nothing.

title: The Deduction That Changes Nothing
description: A proportional rate with full loss relief leaves lesson 67 at 589 trades whatever the rate. Relieve none of the losses and the same tenth of an R stops being an edge at 22.18 per cent.

title: Paying Yourself Before You Know
description: The capital a wage requires is 11.40 years of it at the size lesson 75 licenses and the pace lesson 76 measured, and 88.3 per cent of that capital is drawn before lesson 67 returns a verdict.

title: The Cost That Does Not Scale
description: A cost base a quarter the size of the wage takes a quarter of the edge, which turns lesson 79’s 10.07 years to a verdict into 17.90 at the pace lesson 76 measured and into 1.30 at forty trades a month.

title: What the Book Clears
description: Eleven bars, one book: the two rules module 9 licensed clear four, fail five, and two cannot be answered from anything this course measured. The whole record behind them is seven trades.

title: The Second Way to Disagree
description: A second instrument takes lesson 81’s 1.04 independent bets to 1.28 at the correlation equities actually run at. Turning one leg short takes the same pair’s standard deviation from 0.9810 to 0.1940.

title: The Same Thing in Two Places
description: Lesson 63’s 0.1230 a share is 0.0100 of spread, 0.1030 of slippage and 0.0100 of commission. A second venue competes for 16.3 per cent of it, and a cross-venue difference must clear 11.94 basis points.

title: The Share That Is Real
description: Six habits this course has already priced, put together for the first time. Two of them take the share of accepted rules that are genuinely alive from 43.2 per cent to 6.0.

title: The Unit That Moved
description: Lesson 63 measured R once, at 1.5443 a share. On the first thirty moves it is 2.0446 and on the last twenty-nine it is 0.7543, and every absolute distance in this course is quoted in it.

title: Taking the Profit
description: The same seven trades win six of seven at every profit target on this page, while the money runs from 7.64 a share to 11.74. The exit setting is worth 98.5 per cent of what the entry rule earned, and the win rate cannot see it.

title: The Second Exit
description: Every stop from half an R outward leaves lesson 63's record untouched, because the rule's own exit always arrives first. At a quarter of an R it fires on two trades, both winners, and 9.84 a share becomes 3.94.

title: The Size of the Next One
description: Flat sizing returns 9.839 a share in all 5,040 orders these seven trades could have arrived in. Doubling after a win and halving after a loss returns 0.5631 of what its own average position earned, and wins in 1,741 orders of 5,040.

title: The Money That Was Showing
description: The seven trades showed 14.60 a share at their best closes and paid 10.70. The 3.90 that was on the screen and left is 26.7 per cent of everything that ever showed, and four of the seven trades give back none of it.

title: The Four Habits Together
description: Alone the early exit costs 2.20 a share and a quarter-R stop costs 5.90, which should leave 1.74. Run together they leave 4.44, because two exits compete rather than stack, and the rule worth 4.16 over holding ends worth minus 1.24.

title: What the Whole Grid Earns
description: All 253 of lesson 63's rules, held at once, make 4.16 a share over twenty-eight moves. One rule drawn at random makes 4.10 at the median. The diversifying bought 4.21 per cent of standard deviation and no return at all, and holding makes 6.60.

title: Where the Result Came From
description: Three of the four-rule book's twenty-eight moves are 80.5 per cent of everything it made, and taking them out leaves 0.80. Buying and holding is the less concentrated of the two, at 57.6 per cent.

title: The Rule That Trades the Most
description: Put the 0.1230 round trip back and the book's 4.10 becomes 3.70, and the ranking inside it inverts. The best rule on the grid net of its own turnover is a 3-bar average against a 12 that never changes position at all.

title: The Ride You Actually Bought
description: The four-rule book's worst run is 1.85 a share against 2.10 for the best rule inside it: 88.1 per cent of the pain for 83.7 per cent of the return. The slowest member alone runs 1.10 and beats the book on every column.

title: The Book on One Card
description: Delete one member at a time and three of the four deletions improve the book. All four three-rule books lose to the slowest member run alone, which nets 3.98 on one position change against the book's 3.70 on thirteen.
